# Synchronization {background-color="#40666e"}

## Questions to consider
:::{.nonincremental}
- What are the requirements for a critical section synchronization solution, and how do bounded waiting and progress differ?
- Why do naive implementations like a simple boolean lock fail, and what must happen atomically instead?
- What are the practical limitations of Peterson's solution, and why don't they work well on modern architectures?
:::

## Problem
- Two processes accessing a reservation system, where the number of open seats is tracked by a counter
  - A: Releasing Seat
  - B: Reserving Seat
- Counter at 10; Process A `counter++ (10 -> 11);` Process B `counter-- (10 -> 9);`
- What could go wrong?
  ```{.c}
  mov 0x8049a1c, %eax
  add $0x1, %eax
  mov %eax, 0x8049a1c

  mov 0x8049a1c, %eax
  sub $0x1, %eax
  mov %eax, 0x8049a1c
  ```

## Race conditions
- If interleaved, whoever goes last wins. Either way, 11 or 9 is an incorrect value. This is a [race condition]{.alert}
- Very common in multi-programming environments: allocating disk blocks or memory pages, writing to a file, network buffers, etc.
- How can we solve race conditions?
  - [Mutual Exclusion]{.alert} (one at a time) on [Critical Sections]{.alert} (the contention data/code)

## Challenges we face
- How large should a critical section be?
- How long can a process be in a critical section
  - What happens if they crash while within a critical section?
- How do we implement? Who enforces entrance into critical sections?

## Beware naïve implementations
- Why not use a simple bool?
  ```{.c}
  bool lock = FALSE
  do {
    while (lock == TRUE);
    lock = TRUE;
    //CRITICAL SECTION
    lock = FALSE;
  }while(TRUE);
  ```

- This implementation requires TWO operations: a read (test) and a write (set) that must be atomic

## Critical section solution requirements
- [Mutual exclusion]{.alert}
- [Progress]{.alert}
- [Bounded waiting]{.alert}


## Requirement 1: Mutual exclusion
:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%" .smaller}
- [Safety]{.alert} property for the *system*::At most one process in the CS at any instant
- Traffic light: cross streets are **never** green at the same time. One double green, even for an instant, breaks it
- To show it's violated: find **one** interleaving that puts two processes in the CS
- To show it holds: argue that *no* interleaving can (one lucky run proves nothing)
- The naïve `bool` lock fails: both processes can read `lock == FALSE` before either one sets it
:::

::: {.column width="2%"}
:::

::: {.column width="43%"}
| Step | $P_0$ | $P_1$ | `lock` |
|:-:|:--|:--|:-:|
| 1 | reads `lock`: F, leaves `while` | | F |
| 2 | *preempted* | reads `lock`: F, leaves `while` | F |
| 3 | | `lock = TRUE`, enters CS | T |
| 4 | *resumes*: `lock = TRUE` (no re-check) | in CS | T |
| 5 | enters CS | in CS | T |

**Both in the CS.**
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
- Same race as the `counter++` example at the start: read, get preempted, write based on what you read earlier.
- The gap between the test (step 1) and the set (step 4) is the whole problem. Atomicity would close it.
- At step 4, `lock` is already TRUE, so writing TRUE changes nothing. P0 never looks again; it already passed the test.
- Stress the asymmetry: one bad interleaving disproves ME. Proving it takes a reasoning argument over all interleavings, which we'll do for Peterson's.
- Calling it a "safety" property sets up the contrast with Progress and Bounded Waiting, which are about "something good eventually happens" (liveness).
- Trivial solution that satisfies ME: never let anyone in. That's why ME alone isn't enough. Segue to Progress.
- Traffic light version: a light stuck red in every direction never shows two greens. Perfectly safe, totally useless.
:::

## Requirement 2: Progress
- [Liveness]{.alert} property for the *system*: if the CS is empty and someone wants in, **someone** gets in
  - Traffic light: if the intersection is empty and a car is waiting, **some** direction eventually gets a green. The all-red light fails this
- Two parts to the rule:
  - A process that **isn't trying to enter** can't keep anyone else out
  - If several processes are trying to enter, one of them gets in. They can't all wait on each other forever
- Test for a violation: Is the CS empty? Is someone trying to get in? Are they stuck anyway?
  - Three yeses means Progress is violated

::: {.notes}
- Mutual exclusion alone is easy: never let anyone in. Progress is what rules that out.
- The "finite time" part rules out schemes where the contenders keep deferring to each other forever. Don't expand on it here: it's the answer to the upcoming discussion.
:::

## Progress example: strict alternation
:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{.c}
// shared: int turn = 0;
// P_i's code (j is the other)
do {
  while (turn != i);
  //CRITICAL SECTION
  turn = j;
  //REMAINDER
} while (TRUE);
```
- Mutual exclusion ✓: `turn` can't be `0` and `1` at once
- CS empty ✓, $P_0$ wants in ✓, $P_0$ stuck ✓
- Progress ✗
:::

::: {.column width="2%"}
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
| Step | $P_0$ | $P_1$ | `turn` |
|:-:|:--|:--|:-:|
| 1 | in CS | in remainder | 0 |
| 2 | `turn = 1` | in remainder | 1 |
| 3 | wants in again | in remainder | 1 |
| 4 | stuck in `while` | in remainder | 1 |

:::
::::

::: {.notes}
- P1 isn't contending, but it holds the "key" (turn == 1), so it blocks P0 from its remainder section. That's the first part of the rule.
- Traffic light version: a light that won't switch back to north-south until a car crosses east-west. At 2am with no east-west traffic, the north-south car sits at a red light at an empty intersection forever.
- Strict alternation forces the pattern P0, P1, P0, P1... A process that's faster or needs the CS more often gets held back by one that isn't even contending.
- Keep `turn` in mind. Peterson's reuses it, but only as a tie-breaker when **both** want in.
:::

## Requirement 3: Bounded waiting
- [Liveness]{.alert} property for *each process*: once $P_i$ asks to enter, only a bounded number $k$ of other entries can happen before $P_i$ gets its turn
  - Progress says *someone* gets in. Bounded waiting says *you* eventually get in
  - The bound is a **count of entries**, not a time. We can't assume anything about CPU speed
- Traffic light: a car on the side street gets a green within $k$ light cycles. A light that always favors the busy main road starves the side street, even though traffic is always moving
- Violating it means [starvation]{.alert}
- Fix idea: take a number (FIFO), like a deli counter. Then $k = n - 1$

::: {.notes}
- Deli counter: without tickets, whoever pushes hardest gets served, and a polite customer can wait forever even though the counter is always busy.
- For two processes the best possible bound is k = 1: once I'm waiting, you get in at most once more before I do. We'll show Peterson's achieves this.
:::

## Bounded waiting example: $P_0$ always wins
:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Suppose a lock (whatever its implementation) always lets $P_0$ win a tie
- Mutual exclusion ✓
- Progress ✓: the CS is never idle while someone waits
- Bounded waiting ✗: $P_1$ can lose every time
:::

::: {.column width="2%"}
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
| Time | $P_0$ | $P_1$ |
|:-:|:--|:--|
| 1 | in CS | requests entry |
| 2 | exits, re-requests | waiting |
| 3 | **wins tie**, in CS | waiting |
| 4 | exits, re-requests | waiting |
| 5 | **wins tie**, in CS | waiting |
| ... | ... | waiting forever |
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
- Ask: does this violate Progress? No. The CS is in use the whole time, so the *system* is making progress. Only P1 isn't. That's the difference between the two requirements.
- Traffic light version: P0 is the main road with a steady stream of cars, P1 is the side street. Cars are always crossing (Progress ✓), but the side-street car never gets its green (Bounded waiting ✗).
- Preview: the plain test_and_set spinlock later today has this exact problem. Let students find it themselves on that slide.
:::

## Progress vs. bounded waiting
| | [Progress]{.alert} | [Bounded waiting]{.alert} |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Protects | the **system** | **each** process |
| Promise | **someone** gets in | **you** get in |
| Traffic light | an empty intersection with a waiting car doesn't stay red | the side street gets a green within $k$ cycles |
| Failure | CS sits **empty** while processes wait (deadlock) | CS stays **busy**, but one process never gets a turn (starvation) |

- Quick test: **is the CS being used?**
  - Empty and someone's stuck → Progress violated
  - Busy, but the same process keeps losing → Bounded waiting violated

::: {.notes}
- Progress is about the light working at all. Bounded waiting is about the light being fair.
- Neither implies the other: "P0 always wins" has Progress but not Bounded waiting. A deadlocked lock fails Progress, and bounded waiting is moot because nobody gets in.
- Ask students to classify: (a) both processes spin forever with the CS empty, (b) a fast process keeps grabbing the lock ahead of a slow one.
:::

## Discussion: Break this lock
:::{.nonincremental}

- This is $P_i$'s code (swap `i` and `j` for $P_j$). Which of the three requirements does it **meet**, and which does it **violate**? 
- How would you fix it?
:::

```{.c}
// shared: bool flag[2] = {FALSE, FALSE};
do {
  flag[i] = TRUE;
  while (flag[j]);
  //CRITICAL SECTION
  flag[i] = FALSE;
  //REMAINDER
} while (TRUE);
```
::: {.notes}
- **Mutual exclusion holds:** to be in the CS, $P_i$ must have seen `flag[j] == FALSE` *after* setting its own flag, so both can't get in.
- **Progress fails (deadlock):** $P_i$ sets `flag[i] = TRUE`, context switch, $P_j$ sets `flag[j] = TRUE`. Now both spin forever on `while (flag[other])` and nobody is in the CS.
- **Bounded waiting** is moot once it deadlocks.
- If someone says it violates mutual exclusion: have them try to build the interleaving. Setting the flag *before* testing is what saves it. Contrast with the naive bool lock, which tests before setting.

**Fixes students usually propose, in order:**

1. **Check first, then raise your flag.** That's the naive bool lock again: both see the other's flag down, both raise, both enter. Fixes Progress, breaks ME.
2. **Back off:** if the other flag is up, lower yours, wait, raise it again. Both can do this in lockstep forever: raise, see, lower, raise... That's **livelock**. Nobody is blocked, nobody gets in, so Progress still fails. Random backoff makes it unlikely, not impossible.
3. **Add a tie-breaker `turn`, checked only when both flags are up:** `flag[i] = TRUE; turn = j; while (flag[j] && turn == j);`
   - Other process not trying → `flag[j]` is FALSE, walk straight in (strict alternation failed this)
   - Both trying → `turn` holds one value, so exactly one gets in; the last writer waits (flags-only failed this)

**Bridge to Peterson's:** strict alternation used only `turn` and failed when one process wasn't trying. This lock uses only flags and fails when both are trying. Peterson's uses both: flags say who wants in, `turn` breaks the tie.
:::

## Peterson's solution
- Two processes: $P_i$ and $P_j$
- Two shared data items: `int turn; bool flag[2];`
  ```{.c}
  Pis code:
  do {
    flag[i] = TRUE;                // I want to enter critical section
    turn = j;                      // let Pj go first if it wants
    while (flag[j] && turn == j);  // busy wait
    //CRITICAL SECTION
    flag[i] = FALSE;               // Im leaving critical section
    //REMAINDER
  }while(TRUE);
  ```
  - turn is a tie-breaker: if both want in, the last one to write it lets the other go first
  - if `flag[i] == true` → $P_i$ is ready for the critical section
- To enter: $P_i$ sets `flag[i] = true` and `turn = j`
  - i.e., $P_i$ demurs to $P_j$; if they are both ready turn will get set to?
    - Whoever runs last sets the turn to the other process

## Peterson's solution: mutual exclusion
::: {style="font-size: 0.75em"}
```{.c}
Pis code:
do {
  flag[i] = TRUE;                // I want to enter critical section
  turn = j;                      // let Pj go first if it wants
  while (flag[j] && turn == j);  // busy wait
  //CRITICAL SECTION
  flag[i] = FALSE;               // Im leaving critical section
  //REMAINDER
}while(TRUE);
```
:::
- Can both processes be in the CS at the same time?
  - $P_i$ gets past its `while` only if `flag[j] == FALSE` or `turn == i`
  - Suppose both are in the CS. Look at who wrote `turn` **last**, say $P_i$ (it wrote `turn = j`)
    - $P_j$ already set `flag[j] = TRUE` before its own `turn = i`, and nobody touches `turn` again
    - So $P_i$ sees `flag[j] == TRUE && turn == j` and spins until $P_j$ leaves. Contradiction
  - Both say "after you"; the **last** one to say it is the one who waits

::: {.notes}
Concrete trace to draw on the board (both want in at once):

1. P0: `flag[0] = T`
2. P1: `flag[1] = T`
3. P0: `turn = 1`
4. P1: `turn = 0`  ← last writer
5. P0 checks `flag[1] && turn == 1` → T && F → **enters**
6. P1 checks `flag[0] && turn == 0` → T && T → **spins**

Swap the order of steps 3 and 4 and P1 enters instead. Either way exactly one gets in. If only one wants in, the other's flag is FALSE and it walks straight through.
:::

## Peterson's solution: progress
::: {style="font-size: 0.75em"}
```{.c}
Pis code:
do {
  flag[i] = TRUE;                // I want to enter critical section
  turn = j;                      // let Pj go first if it wants
  while (flag[j] && turn == j);  // busy wait
  //CRITICAL SECTION
  flag[i] = FALSE;               // Im leaving critical section
  //REMAINDER
}while(TRUE);
```
:::
- If the CS is empty and someone wants in, does someone get in?
  - $P_j$ not trying: `flag[j]` is FALSE, so $P_i$ walks straight in (strict alternation failed this)
  - Both trying: `turn` is either `i` or `j`, so one of the two `while` conditions is false and that process enters (flags-only deadlocked here)

## Peterson's solution: bounded waiting
::: {style="font-size: 0.75em"}
```{.c}
Pis code:
do {
  flag[i] = TRUE;                // I want to enter critical section
  turn = j;                      // let Pj go first if it wants
  while (flag[j] && turn == j);  // busy wait
  //CRITICAL SECTION
  flag[i] = FALSE;               // Im leaving critical section
  //REMAINDER
}while(TRUE);
```
:::
- Once $P_i$ is waiting, how many times can $P_j$ get in first?
  - At most **once**. To get back in, $P_j$ must set `turn = i`, which lets $P_i$ through and makes $P_j$ wait


::: {.notes}
- Contrast with "P0 always wins": there the winner re-requested and won the tie again. In Peterson's, re-requesting means saying "after you" again, so the waiting process wins.
- Traffic light version: once the side-street car is waiting, the main road gets at most one more green.
- Bounded waiting trace: P_i is spinning (flag[j] T, turn == j). P_j exits, sets flag[j] = F (P_i may slip in right here). P_j wants back in: flag[j] = T, turn = i. Now P_i's condition is `T && F` → enters; P_j's is `T && T` → spins.
:::

## Peterson's solution (cont'd)
```{.c}
Pis code:
do {
  flag[i] = TRUE;                // I want to enter critical section
  turn = j;                      // let Pj go first if it wants
  while (flag[j] && turn == j);  // busy wait
  //CRITICAL SECTION
  flag[i] = FALSE;               // Im leaving critical section
  //REMAINDER
}while(TRUE);
```
- Do you see any issues with this solution?
  - Limitation: Only works for two processes
  - Modern architectures may also break this solution
    - Processors and/or compilers can reorder reads and writes that have no dependencies
    - Multithreaded applications could lead to issues
